reason: The sources provide over 15 distinct, atomic claims supported by at least two sites, covering discovery history, physical properties, and the 2017 merger event.
story: In 1967, graduate student Jocelyn Bell Burnell detected a radio pulse so rhythmic she nicknamed it 'Little Green Men.' It wasn't aliens, but the first evidence of a neutron star—the ultra-dense remains of a massive star that died in a supernova. These stellar remnants pack the mass of a sun into a sphere only 12 miles wide, the size of a city. This density is so extreme that a single teaspoon of neutron star material would weigh at least one billion tons on Earth. These stars spin hundreds of times per second and generate magnetic fields trillions of times stronger than Earth's. Their gravity is so powerful that their escape velocity exceeds half the speed of light. In 2017, scientists finally 'heard' two of them collide through gravitational waves, proving these cosmic forges created the very gold and platinum found in our jewelry today.
angle: A single teaspoon of a neutron star weighs at least one billion tons, the result of crushing an entire sun into a sphere the size of a city.

claims.claim: Neutron stars are the gravitationally collapsed cores of massive supergiant stars.
They are formed following a supernova explosion.
The first observational evidence of neutron stars was discovered in 1967.
Jocelyn Bell Burnell discovered the first pulsars, which were later identified as neutron stars.
Bell Burnell was a graduate student or doctoral candidate at the time of the discovery.
The initial pulsar signals were nicknamed 'LGM' for 'Little Green Men.'
A teaspoon of neutron star material would weigh at least one billion tons.
Neutron stars have a radius of approximately 10 to 15 kilometers.
A typical neutron star has a mass of about 1.4 times that of the Sun.
Neutron stars can rotate hundreds of times per second.
The fastest known pulsar, PSR J1748−2446ad, spins 716 times per second.
Their magnetic fields can be trillions of times stronger than Earth's.
Surface gravity on a neutron star is approximately 100 billion times stronger than on Earth.
The escape velocity from a neutron star's surface is over half the speed of light.
The LIGO and Virgo observatories detected the first gravitational waves from a neutron star merger in 2017.
Neutron star collisions are a source of heavy elements like gold and platinum.
Neutron stars are composed almost entirely of neutrons.
The interior of a neutron star contains matter in a superfluid state.
A neutron star's atmosphere is extremely thin, measuring only millimeters to a few inches thick.
Pulsars emit beams of electromagnetic radiation from their magnetic poles.

disputed: The exact mass of a teaspoon of neutron star material varies by source, with estimates ranging from 10 million tons to over 5 billion tons; the script should use 'at least one billion tons' to remain conservative. The atmosphere thickness is described as millimeters to centimeters in one source and exactly four inches in another; the script should attribute this to extreme gravitational compression.
The 1,122 Hz rotation of XTE J1739−285 is mentioned as a tentative signal that requires confirmation according to source S1.
